subtype: Approach: rigid plan that ignores change [Pitfall]
passage: My name is Vikas, and for years a page was taped above my desk: junior accountant, senior accountant, audit manager, each with a date. When Alka told me a team was forming around reporting tools and asked if I'd join, I said no at once. It wasn't on my page. I told myself the page was the whole point. Two years on, the audit posts I was aiming for are fewer, and the openings I read now list skills I never picked up. Alka's team has doubled in size. I still have the page, but I look at it differently. Last week I finally asked Alka what the team has been learning.

qa.q: What was taped above Vikas's desk?
qa.a: A page with a career path on it: junior accountant, senior accountant and audit manager, each with a date.

qa.q: What was Vikas thinking when turning down the offer so fast?
qa.a: Vikas believed the page was the whole point, so anything off it felt like a threat and was refused at once, a rigid and wary stance.

qa.q: What alternative approach could have helped Vikas, and why?
qa.a: Vikas could have tried a short trial with the new team while keeping the page, because a look at the market would have shown the audit path was shrinking.

qa.q: How might Alka have felt hearing that quick no?
qa.a: Alka may have felt disappointed or puzzled, having offered a place and then watched the team double without Vikas.

grounding: Shows a person holding a fixed career plan, refusing a new opportunity in a growing area, and finding the planned path has fewer openings.

passage:
Manager's note for Bhavna's file, March.
Two years ago I offered Bhavna a move to our new cloud data team. She said no, politely. 'It isn't in my five-year plan. I'm going deep in on-premise databases.' She showed me the plan, printed and laminated. I respected the discipline and didn't push.
Today we discussed the restructure. Most on-premise work moves to the cloud by next year, and her role is being merged. She was quiet for a long time, then said, 'I followed the plan exactly.' She did. The plan just didn't follow the world.
We agreed she will join the cloud team's training batch in April, and I've paired her with Ravi there. I told her the skills she has still count; she will just carry them somewhere new.
Ankita

qa.q: Which team did Ankita offer Bhavna two years ago?
What was Bhavna feeling when she said 'I followed the plan exactly'?
qa.a: She was shaken and hurt, feeling that her discipline had been punished rather than rewarded.

qa.q: What could Bhavna do differently with her plan from now on?
qa.a: She could review it each year against where the field is heading, and treat a new opportunity as a reason to update the plan rather than refuse it.

qa.q: How might Ankita feel looking back at the refused offer?
qa.a: Ankita may feel some regret for not pushing harder, which may be why Bhavna is now paired with Ravi.

grounding: It shows a manager's note on an employee who treated a five-year plan as fixed, refused a growing area and later found the planned path shrinking.

passage:
Friday, 14 November
Bhupen got the lead role on the AI tools team today. Two years ago the same offer came to me first. I said no because my plan, the one on my wall, said 'Year 3: senior mobile developer'. Mobile was the map. AI was off the map.
Today my manager told me the mobile team is shrinking to four people next year. I stood in the parking lot feeling stupid, holding a coffee I didn't drink.
I'm not angry at Bhupen. He said yes to something uncertain. I said no to protect a sheet of paper.
Tomorrow I'm taking the plan off the wall. Not throwing it away. Just writing on top of it, in pencil: 'Review every six months. Anything new gets a real look.'
Damini

qa.q: What did Damini's plan say for year 3?
How did Damini feel in the parking lot?
qa.a: Damini felt stupid and regretful, seeing that the rigid plan had cost the chance Bhupen took.

qa.q: What other approach does Damini's pencil note bring?
qa.a: Reviewing the plan every six months and giving new chances a real look, so the plan can change as the field does.

qa.q: How might Bhupen feel if he learnt Damini had turned the role down first?
qa.a: Bhupen might feel awkward or sympathetic, knowing his gain came from an offer Damini refused.

grounding: It shows someone who refused an opportunity in a growing area because it was off the plan, and two years later finds the planned path shrinking.
